title: CPU & Fetch-Decode-Execute
tagline: The three-step loop a CPU repeats billions of times per second to run every program you use.

sections.content:
Every program you have ever run — a web browser, a video game, a machine learning model — is ultimately executed by one relentlessly simple process: a CPU repeatedly fetching an instruction from memory, figuring out what it means, and carrying it out. This **fetch-decode-execute cycle** is the heartbeat of every computer, running billions of times per second, yet each individual cycle is entirely mechanical and rule-based.

Understanding this cycle answers questions you might have wondered about: Why does an infinite loop freeze a program? Why does a function call take time? Why can multi-core CPUs run programs faster? What does a 3.5 GHz clock speed actually mean? All of these trace back to how the CPU processes instructions one step at a time.

This chapter builds the full picture from components to cycle to optimisation. We cover: the key CPU components (ALU, registers, control unit, program counter, instruction register), what an instruction actually is, the fetch-decode-execute cycle in detailed step-by-step form, the role of the clock, instruction sets and ISAs, and an introduction to pipelining — the technique that makes modern CPUs run multiple instructions simultaneously.

A note on level: we will be precise but will not go all the way down to transistors (that was the previous chapter). We are operating at the **architecture** level — the logical design of how the CPU works, which is the level that matters for understanding performance, compilers, and operating systems.

sections.title: The CPU as an Extremely Focused Chef
sections.content:
Imagine a chef in a restaurant kitchen. There is a **recipe book** (main memory — RAM) that contains every instruction for every dish. The chef has a tiny countertop (registers) where they can hold only a few ingredients at once. They have a **notepad** with a finger pointing to the current step (the Program Counter). And they have a single focused brain that can only do one operation at a time: read the next step from the recipe, understand what it means, and do it.

The chef's process: look at the notepad to find the current recipe line (fetch), read and interpret that line — 'whisk the eggs' means something different from 'preheat the oven' (decode), then actually perform the action (execute). After each step, the finger on the notepad moves to the next line.

The CPU is this chef, but operating at three billion steps per second, with a recipe book that can hold billions of lines (instructions), and a countertop that can hold only a few dozen values (registers) at any time. The 'recipe steps' are binary machine instructions, and the 'actions' are arithmetic, memory reads/writes, and jumps to other parts of the recipe.

sections.title: The Key CPU Components
sections.content:
Before tracing the fetch-decode-execute cycle, we need to understand the major components involved:

**Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)**: The part of the CPU that actually computes. The ALU takes two inputs and an operation code, and produces a result. Operations include: ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV (arithmetic), AND, OR, XOR, NOT (bitwise logic), and CMP (compare — subtraction where only the flags are kept). The ALU is built from the logic gates we studied in the previous chapter: adders for arithmetic, gate arrays for logic. It is purely combinational — no memory, no state. Given inputs, it instantly produces outputs.

**Registers**: Extremely fast, small storage locations inside the CPU itself. A typical modern CPU has 16-32 general-purpose registers, each holding one word (32 or 64 bits). Registers are the only operands the ALU can directly work with. If you want to add two numbers that are in RAM, you must first load them into registers, then add. Registers are on the same die as the ALU — access time is roughly 0.3 nanoseconds.

**Special-purpose registers** include:
- **Program Counter (PC)** — holds the memory address of the *next* instruction to fetch
- **Instruction Register (IR)** — holds the instruction currently being decoded/executed
- **Stack Pointer (SP)** — tracks the top of the call stack
- **Status/Flags Register** — records results of the last operation: Zero flag (result was 0), Carry flag (unsigned overflow), Sign flag (result was negative), Overflow flag (signed overflow)

**Control Unit (CU)**: The 'traffic controller' of the CPU. It reads the instruction from the IR, decodes it into a sequence of micro-operations, and sends control signals to every other component — telling the ALU which operation to perform, telling multiplexers which data path to activate, directing reads and writes to memory. Modern CPUs implement the CU as a microcode ROM for complex instructions.

**Memory interface (MAR + MDR)**: The CPU communicates with RAM through the **Memory Address Register** (MAR — which address to access) and **Memory Data Register** (MDR — the data read from or to be written to that address). These act as the CPU's 'hands' reaching out to the slower memory system.

**Bus**: The wired pathway connecting the CPU to memory and I/O devices. The **address bus** carries which address to access; the **data bus** carries the data being transferred; the **control bus** carries signals like READ or WRITE. The width of the data bus (32-bit or 64-bit) determines how many bits can be transferred per cycle.

sections.title: What Is an Instruction?
sections.content:
An instruction is a fixed-length (or sometimes variable-length) binary pattern that the CPU hardware recognises and knows how to carry out. Every instruction has:

**Opcode**: A binary code identifying the operation. ADD, SUB, LOAD, STORE, JUMP each have a unique opcode. On a 32-bit MIPS CPU, the opcode is 6 bits — giving 64 possible instruction types.

**Operands**: Which registers or immediate values (constants encoded directly in the instruction) to use. A MIPS instruction like `add R1, R2, R3` specifies three register operands.

**Addressing mode**: How to interpret operands. Common modes:
- *Register*: the value in a register (`R1`)
- *Immediate*: a constant encoded in the instruction (`#42`)
- *Direct*: a fixed memory address (`[0x4000]`)
- *Indirect (register)*: the memory address held in a register (`[R2]`)
- *Displacement*: base register plus an offset (`[R2 + 8]`) — the most common mode for accessing struct fields and array elements

A typical program in memory looks like: a sequence of these binary instruction patterns, laid out end-to-end starting at some load address. The program counter points into this sequence.

**Machine code vs. assembly vs. high-level language**: Machine code is raw binary instructions. Assembly language is human-readable names for those instructions (`ADD R0, R1, R2` instead of `00000000001000100000000000100000`). High-level languages like Python or JavaScript are translated — by compilers or interpreters — down through several layers until eventually machine code executes on the CPU.

sections.title: The Fetch Phase: Getting the Next Instruction
sections.content:
The fetch phase is the first step of the cycle. Its job is to retrieve the next instruction from memory.

**Step F1**: The CPU copies the value in the **Program Counter** (PC) into the **Memory Address Register** (MAR). This tells the memory system which address to read.

**Step F2**: The CPU sends a READ signal on the control bus. The memory system (after its latency — perhaps 4 clock cycles for an L1 cache hit) places the instruction bytes onto the data bus, and the CPU reads them into the **Memory Data Register** (MDR).

**Step F3**: The contents of the MDR are copied into the **Instruction Register** (IR). The instruction is now sitting inside the CPU, ready to be decoded.

**Step F4**: The PC is **incremented** by the size of the instruction (e.g., 4 bytes on a 32-bit fixed-width ISA like MIPS or RISC-V). This advances the 'bookmark' to the next instruction before the current one has even finished executing — important for pipelining.

The entire fetch phase takes a varying number of clock cycles depending on where the instruction is in the memory hierarchy. If it is in the L1 instruction cache (which it usually is for sequential code), it might be available in 4 cycles. If it must be fetched from RAM, it might take 200+ cycles — a 50x penalty that makes cache misses one of the biggest performance costs in modern systems.

sections.title: The Decode Phase: Interpreting the Instruction
sections.content:
With the instruction sitting in the Instruction Register, the **Control Unit** decodes it. Decoding means: 'what does this binary pattern mean, and what signals do I need to send to execute it?'

For a simple RISC architecture, decoding is fast and uniform. Fixed-length instructions (all 32 bits wide in MIPS) mean the control unit always knows exactly where the opcode field, source register fields, and destination register fields are — decoding can be done with simple bit extraction:

- Bits 31-26: opcode (6 bits)
- Bits 25-21: source register 1 (5 bits = addresses up to 32 registers)
- Bits 20-16: source register 2 or destination (5 bits)
- Bits 15-0: immediate value or address offset (16 bits)

The control unit decodes the opcode into a set of **control signals** — wires that will tell each component what to do during the execute phase. For example, an ADD instruction decodes into:
- 'ALU operation: ADD'
- 'Read source operands from registers R1 and R2'
- 'Write result back to register R3'
- 'Do not access memory'

**Complex instruction sets (CISC)** like x86 have variable-length instructions (1 to 15 bytes on x86-64) and many addressing modes. Decoding is much harder — modern Intel CPUs actually translate x86 instructions into simpler internal micro-operations (micro-ops) before executing them, effectively running a RISC engine inside a CISC wrapper.

For most student-level study, you will work with RISC architectures (MIPS, RISC-V, ARM) where decoding is conceptually clean.

sections.title: The Execute Phase: Doing the Work
sections.content:
Execution is where the actual computation happens. The control signals generated during decode are sent to all the relevant components simultaneously. What 'execute' means depends entirely on the instruction type:

**Arithmetic/logic instructions** (ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, SHL, SHR):
- The source register values are fed as inputs to the ALU
- The control unit tells the ALU which operation to perform
- The ALU output is written to the destination register
- The Flags register is updated (zero, carry, sign, overflow)
- Time: typically 1-4 clock cycles

**Load instruction** (LDR R1, [R2+8] — load the value at address R2+8 into R1):
- The ALU computes the effective address: R2 + 8
- The address is placed in MAR
- A READ is issued on the control bus
- The data comes back through MDR into R1
- Time: 1 cycle if L1 cache hit; 200+ cycles if RAM miss

**Store instruction** (STR R1, [R2+8] — write R1 to address R2+8):
- Effective address computed, placed in MAR
- R1 copied to MDR
- WRITE issued on control bus
- Time: similar to load

**Branch instruction** (BEQ R1, R2, label — branch to label if R1 equals R2):
- The ALU compares R1 and R2 (SUB and check zero flag)
- If the condition holds, the PC is set to the branch target address
- If not, the PC was already incremented during fetch; execution continues sequentially
- The branch target is typically computed as PC + offset (PC-relative addressing)

**Jump instruction** (J target — unconditional jump):
- The PC is set to the target address, overriding the incremented value

After execute completes, the cycle begins again. The new PC value (either the incremented address or a branch target) is copied to MAR, and fetch begins for the next instruction.

sections.label: CPU Simulator
sections.explanation: This simulator shows the structural separation of fetch, decode, and execute as distinct methods called in a loop. The PC advances during fetch (before execute completes), mirroring real CPUs where the PC always points to the *next* unexecuted instruction. The HALT instruction breaks the while loop — in a real CPU it would put the processor into a low-power idle state waiting for an interrupt.

sections.title: The Clock: The CPU's Heartbeat
sections.content:
All of the above happens in synchronisation with a **clock** — a crystal oscillator that generates a precise, stable square wave (alternating 0V and high voltage). Every edge of this wave triggers the next step in the CPU's sequential logic.

A **3.5 GHz** clock produces 3,500,000,000 oscillations per second — one cycle every ~0.286 nanoseconds. Every component in the CPU is designed to complete its operation within one (or a fixed number of) clock cycles.

The **CPI (Cycles Per Instruction)** is the average number of clock cycles each instruction takes. On older simple architectures, every instruction took exactly 1 cycle (CPI = 1). Modern superscalar CPUs can execute multiple instructions per cycle (CPI < 1, or equivalently IPC — instructions per cycle > 1). Cache misses, branch mispredictions, and data dependencies all increase the effective CPI.

**CPU performance** is often summarised as: Time = Instructions × CPI × (1/Clock_Frequency). A faster clock helps, but so does reducing CPI (better architecture) and reducing instruction count (better compilers and algorithms).

The clock frequency is limited by two physics constraints: (1) **signal propagation delay** — electrons take real time to travel through transistors, and (2) **heat** — faster switching generates more heat than can be dissipated. Clock speeds plateaued around 3-5 GHz in the mid-2000s for this reason. The industry responded by adding **multiple cores** — running several independent CPUs on one chip — and by deep **pipelining** and other ILP techniques.

sections.title: Instruction Set Architectures: The CPU's Contract
sections.content:
An **Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)** is the specification of all instructions a processor family understands: their binary encoding, their semantics, the number and width of registers, memory addressing modes, and the conventions for system calls. The ISA is the interface between hardware and software — programs compiled for one ISA will run on any CPU that implements that ISA, regardless of the underlying microarchitecture.

Major ISA families:

**x86 / x86-64**: Originally Intel's 16-bit ISA from 1978, evolved through 32-bit (IA-32) to 64-bit (AMD64/EM64T). Used in virtually all desktop and server CPUs. Famously **CISC** — complex instructions, variable lengths, many addressing modes. Has accumulated decades of backwards-compatible cruft.

**ARM**: Dominant in mobile and embedded devices. Originally a simple **RISC** design (Advanced RISC Machines). ARM64 (AArch64) is the current 64-bit version, now also used in Apple M-series laptop chips and Amazon Graviton server chips. Energy-efficient and clean ISA.

**RISC-V**: An open-source ISA developed at UC Berkeley from 2010. Increasingly popular for embedded and research. Clean, modular, and free to implement without royalties.

**MIPS**: Once dominant in Unix workstations and still used in embedded systems and routers. Taught in most computer architecture courses because of its clean 32-bit fixed-width instruction format.

**The RISC vs. CISC distinction** has blurred. Modern Intel CPUs translate CISC x86 instructions into internal RISC-like micro-ops and execute those. Meanwhile, ARM includes instructions that are more complex than classic RISC. The ISA is now a compatibility interface; the internal execution engine is whatever is fastest.

sections.title: Pipelining: Running Multiple Instructions at Once
sections.content:
A non-pipelined CPU must complete the entire fetch-decode-execute cycle for one instruction before starting the next. This is like a car factory that builds one complete car before touching the next — extremely inefficient.

**Pipelining** breaks the cycle into discrete stages and overlaps them. A classic 5-stage MIPS pipeline:

1. **IF** (Instruction Fetch): Fetch instruction from cache
2. **ID** (Instruction Decode / Register Read): Decode opcode, read source registers
3. **EX** (Execute): ALU operation or effective address computation
4. **MEM** (Memory Access): Load from or store to data cache
5. **WB** (Write Back): Write result to destination register

Each stage takes one clock cycle. With five stages processing five different instructions simultaneously, the pipeline can complete one instruction per clock cycle in steady state — a 5x speedup over a purely sequential design.

The analogy is an assembly line: while one car is being painted, the next is being assembled, and the one before that is having its engine installed. All five cars move forward one station per time step.

**Pipeline hazards** are the complications:

**Data hazard (RAW — Read After Write)**: Instruction 2 needs a register that Instruction 1 is still computing. Solution: forwarding (pass the result directly from EX/MEM stage output back to EX input without waiting for WB), or inserting a pipeline stall (bubble).

**Control hazard (branch)**: When a branch is encountered, the CPU does not yet know whether to take it. Meanwhile it has already fetched and started decoding the next sequential instruction. If the branch is taken, those instructions are wrong — they must be flushed and the correct instructions fetched. Modern CPUs use **branch prediction** to guess the outcome and speculatively execute down the predicted path, discarding the work only if the prediction was wrong.

**Structural hazard**: Two instructions need the same hardware resource simultaneously. Solved by duplicating resources or stalling.

Modern CPUs run **14-19 stage** pipelines (Intel's Core architecture has around 14-19 stages) and execute multiple instructions per cycle (**superscalar execution**), with out-of-order execution, register renaming, and sophisticated branch predictors achieving IPC values of 3-6. The simple 3-step cycle we started with is still there conceptually, but massively optimised in its physical realisation.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Deeper Insights
sections.content:
**'Faster clock = faster computer'**: Not necessarily. Clock speed (GHz) is only one factor. Two CPUs at the same clock speed can have very different performance if their IPC (instructions per cycle), cache hierarchy, or ISA efficiency differs. Apple's M1 at 3.2 GHz was often faster than Intel chips at 4+ GHz.

**'Programs execute in the order written'**: Modern CPUs use **out-of-order execution** — they can re-order the execution of instructions (not visible to the programmer) as long as data dependencies are respected. An instruction that would stall (waiting for a cache miss) can be skipped over while later independent instructions execute.

**'The PC always points to the current instruction'**: Actually, after fetch, the PC has already been incremented to the *next* instruction. During branch execution, the branch target overwrites this incremented value if the branch is taken. x86 program counters (called RIP) behave similarly.

**'Branch prediction is always wrong on random code'**: Modern branch predictors (like the perceptron predictor or TAGE predictor) achieve 95-99%+ accuracy on typical workloads by learning patterns. A misprediction costs 15-20 cycles on modern pipelines — significant but relatively rare.

**'Registers are just fast variables'**: Registers are the only storage the ALU can directly operate on. When you write `x + y` in C, the compiler must arrange for `x` and `y` to be in registers at that moment — or generate a load instruction first. Register allocation is one of the hardest problems in compiler construction.

**ENIAC and the stored-program concept**: Early computers (ENIAC, 1945) were programmed by physically rewiring the machine — there was no stored program. John von Neumann's 1945 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC' proposed storing program instructions in the same memory as data. This 'von Neumann architecture' is what all modern fetch-decode-execute CPUs implement. The alternative — Harvard architecture, with separate instruction and data memories — is still used in some embedded microcontrollers and in the L1 cache split of modern CPUs (separate instruction and data caches).

**Performance debugging insights from fetch-decode-execute:**
- A tight loop that reads sequential memory is fast because instructions and data are in L1 cache (short fetch latency).
- A function call is slow relative to inline code because it pushes/pops the stack (memory operations) and may flush the pipeline via a branch.
- Branch-heavy code is slower on modern CPUs than equivalent branchless code (using conditional moves) because branch mispredictions flush the pipeline.
- `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` the branch at `i < n` is predicted correctly almost every time (the loop body runs n times, then exits once) — so loop overhead is minimal.
- The reason `console.log` in a hot loop makes code 10-100x slower is not the logging itself but the side-effects: I/O system calls, string formatting, and memory allocation that disrupt cache and branch predictor state.

items: The CPU contains an **ALU** (computes), **registers** (fast on-chip storage), a **Control Unit** (orchestrates), a **Program Counter** (points to the next instruction), and an **Instruction Register** (holds the current instruction).

The **fetch-decode-execute cycle**: (1) copy PC to MAR, read instruction from memory into IR, increment PC; (2) control unit decodes opcode and operands into control signals; (3) ALU computes, memory is accessed, or PC is changed — then repeat.
The **clock** synchronises all operations. A 3.5 GHz clock ticks 3.5 billion times per second; performance = instructions × CPI × (1/frequency).
An **ISA** (x86, ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) is the specification of all instructions a processor family understands — the contract between hardware and software.
**Pipelining** overlaps fetch, decode, and execute of different instructions simultaneously, targeting one instruction completed per clock cycle in steady state.
**Pipeline hazards** (data, control, structural) require stalling, forwarding, or branch prediction to resolve — branch mispredictions are a major source of performance loss on deep pipelines.
Modern CPUs extend the basic pipeline with superscalar execution, out-of-order execution, and branch prediction to achieve IPC > 1 — multiple instructions completed per clock cycle.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Program Counter (PC)?
options: Counts how many instructions have been executed
Holds the current instruction being decoded
Holds the memory address of the next instruction to fetch
Counts the CPU clock cycles
quiz.explanation: The PC holds the memory address of the NEXT instruction to fetch. After fetch, it is immediately incremented. A branch instruction can override this value to jump to a different address.

quiz.question: In what order do the three phases occur in one CPU cycle?
options: Decode, Fetch, Execute
Execute, Decode, Fetch
Fetch, Execute, Decode
Fetch, Decode, Execute
quiz.explanation: Fetch retrieves the instruction from memory, Decode interprets the binary pattern into control signals, Execute carries out the operation. This order cannot be changed — you must have the instruction before decoding it.

quiz.question: What is the ALU responsible for?
options: Fetching instructions from memory
Performing arithmetic and logic operations on register values
Deciding which instruction to execute next
Managing the connection between CPU and RAM
quiz.explanation: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) performs computations: ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, CMP, and shift operations on values in registers. It is a purely combinational circuit — no memory or state.

quiz.question: What is the Instruction Register (IR) used for?
options: Storing the target address of the next branch
Holding the instruction currently being decoded and executed
Counting executed instructions for performance monitoring
Buffering data being written to memory
quiz.explanation: The IR holds the instruction that was fetched from memory. The Control Unit reads the IR to decode the instruction and generate control signals for the execute phase.

quiz.question: What does a 3.5 GHz clock speed mean for a CPU?
options: It can execute 3.5 billion instructions per second
Its internal clock oscillates 3.5 billion times per second
It transfers 3.5 GB of data per second
It has 3.5 billion transistors
quiz.explanation: GHz means billions of oscillations per second of the clock signal. Instructions per second depends on CPI (cycles per instruction), so 3.5 GHz does not directly mean 3.5 billion instructions per second.

quiz.question: What is a pipeline hazard?
options: A CPU overheating due to high clock speed
A situation where pipeline stages cannot proceed normally, causing stalls or errors
A branch instruction in the middle of a loop
A cache miss that requires fetching from RAM
quiz.explanation: A pipeline hazard occurs when the normal pipeline flow must be interrupted. Types include: data hazards (instruction needs a value not yet computed), control hazards (branches change the PC), and structural hazards (resource conflicts).

quiz.question: What does the RISC acronym stand for, and what is a key characteristic of RISC ISAs?
options: Rapid Instruction Set Computer — instructions execute in parallel
Reduced Instruction Set Computer — small set of fixed-length simple instructions
Registered Instruction Set Computer — all operations use registers
Revised Intel Standard Computer — x86 compatible instruction encoding
quiz.explanation: RISC stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Key traits: small uniform instruction set, fixed-length instructions (e.g., 32 bits in MIPS), load/store architecture (only load/store instructions access memory; all others operate on registers).

quiz.question: What is the purpose of pipelining in a CPU?
options: To execute one instruction faster by using more transistors
To increase clock frequency beyond physical limits
To overlap the fetch, decode, and execute stages of multiple instructions
To reduce the number of registers needed
quiz.explanation: Pipelining overlaps the execution of multiple instructions by having different instructions in different pipeline stages simultaneously. In steady state, one instruction can complete per clock cycle, a 5x speedup for a 5-stage pipeline.

quiz.question: What is 'branch prediction' in the context of CPU pipelines?
options: Sorting branches alphabetically to reduce decode time
Guessing the outcome of a conditional branch to keep the pipeline full
Caching frequently executed branch targets in registers
Replacing branch instructions with arithmetic to avoid pipeline stalls
quiz.explanation: When a conditional branch is encountered, the CPU does not yet know which way to go. Branch prediction guesses the outcome and speculatively fetches and executes instructions from the predicted path. If wrong, the speculatively executed instructions are discarded and the pipeline is refilled from the correct path — costing 15-20 cycles.

quiz.question: In the fetch-decode-execute cycle, when exactly is the PC incremented?
options: After the execute phase completes
During the decode phase
During the fetch phase, before execute begins
Only when a branch instruction is decoded
quiz.explanation: The PC is incremented during the FETCH phase (step F4), after the instruction is copied into the IR. This means the PC already points to the NEXT instruction before the current instruction has been decoded or executed. A branch in the execute phase then overwrites this incremented value if the branch is taken.
